stories.title: ZMC Group Expands Recall of 245,000 Light-Up Toys — Button Battery Ingestion Hazard

x_posts.label: Post 1
x_posts.text:
CPSC: 245,124 ZMC Group light-up toys recalled.

Yo-yos, maracas, wands, LED headbands — button cell batteries. Ingestion can cause severe internal burns.

Stop use. Email recallzmctoy@gmail.com for refund.

#COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
If your kids have light-up toys from dollar stores or party supply shops, this recall is worth checking today.

The CPSC announced an expanded recall of 245,124 battery-powered light-up toys sold by ZMC Group. The products include light-up yo-yos, maracas, wands, and LED headbands — the kind of toys that often show up in goodie bags, party favors, and holiday bins.

The hazard is the button cell battery (a small lithium coin cell) inside the toy. If a child swallows one, it can become lodged in the throat or stomach. The battery then creates an electrical current that causes severe internal burns, serious injury, or death — sometimes within two hours. It's a well-documented hazard, and the CPSC has issued multiple recalls for button-cell-containing products over the past few years.

What to do if you have one of these toys:
- Stop use immediately
- Destroy the toy (so other children can't access it)
- Email recallzmctoy@gmail.com for a full refund

The toys were sold at dollar stores, party supply retailers, and online. If you're not sure whether you have one, look for small light-up toys with a tiny battery compartment that requires a coin or screwdriver to open — that's a sign of a button cell battery.

Have you seen light-up toys like these in your home?
facebook.image_caption: CPSC recall: 245,124 ZMC Group light-up toys recalled for button cell battery hazard. Stop use now — destroy and email for refund.

stories.title: D49 Fall Break Starts October 12 — Plus PTCs This Week and a Board Meeting Tomorrow

x_posts.label: Post 2
x_posts.text:
D49 families: a packed week before fall break.

Board meeting tomorrow (Oct 8). PTCs Thursday (Oct 9). Fall break starts Monday, October 12 — runs through Oct 23.

Check d49.org for your school's PTC sign-up window.

#COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
D49 families, you've got a full week before fall break — and a couple of things to get on your radar for the next 48 hours.

First: the D49 Board of Education meets tomorrow, October 8. The agenda includes an emergency transfer of six online schools that had been operating under a state authorization. If your child is enrolled in one of D49's online programs, it's worth keeping an eye on how that plays out.

Second: parent-teacher conferences are this Thursday, October 9. If you haven't signed up yet, check your school's website or app — sign-up windows can close a few days before.

Then fall break starts Monday, October 12 and runs all the way through Friday, October 23. That's nearly two full weeks — longer than D11's break (which runs October 19-23) and a great window to get outside before the cold sets in. We'll be running an events roundup this week to help D49 families plan.

For your school's exact conference schedule and fall break details, check d49.org.

What do you have planned for fall break?

stories.title: Free This Week in COS: Fossil Day, Costume Exchange, and More Coming Up in October

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text:
COS family events this week and in late October:

Oct 9 — Costume Exchange (free)
Oct 10 — Fossil Day at Garden of the Gods (free)
Oct 24 — Jack-o-Lantern Trail, Palmer Park ($5)
Oct 25 — GoG Trunk-or-Treat (free)

#COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
Here's what's on the COS family calendar for the next few weeks — and the good news is most of it is free.

**This week:**

🦕 **Halloween Costume Exchange (Thursday, Oct 9, free)** — Bring a gently used costume, take one home. A great way to rotate before trick-or-treat season ramps up.

🦕 **National Fossil Day at Garden of the Gods (Friday, Oct 10, free)** — Family-friendly programming celebrating the geology and ancient life of Colorado. If your kiddos have ever asked why the red rocks look the way they do, this is the day for that conversation.

The **Cool Science Festival** is also running through October 18 at venues across Colorado Springs — free programming for curious families throughout the month.

**Coming up in late October:**

🎃 **Jack-o-Lantern Trail at Palmer Park (October 24, $5/person)** — A lit trail through Palmer Park with carved jack-o-lanterns. A rare paid event in the COS fall lineup — but a popular one.

🎃 **Garden of the Gods Trunk-or-Treat (October 25, free)** — One of the better free Halloween events in COS, with one of the most dramatic backdrops.

**Ongoing on Saturdays in October:**

Miner's Pumpkin Patch is open Saturdays through the end of the month if you're looking for a classic fall outing.

These are different events from the ones we covered yesterday (Boo at the Bridge, Pumpkins in the Park, Boo at the Zoo, Halloween History Detectives) — so the full COS October calendar is filling out nicely.

Which event is your family most excited about?

stories.title: AAP Issues New AI Guidance for Pediatric Care — What COS Parents Should Know

x_posts.label: Post 4
x_posts.text:
AAP wrapped its annual conference (Oct 2–6) with new AI guidance for pediatric care.

Also: developmental disability trends study 2019–2024, plus research linking smartphones to depression, obesity, and poor sleep.

#COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
The American Academy of Pediatrics wrapped up its annual conference today (October 2-6), and there are a few takeaways worth knowing as a parent.

The big headline: the AAP released new guidance on artificial intelligence in pediatric care. As AI tools increasingly enter doctor's offices — from AI-assisted diagnosis to automated screening tools — the AAP is laying out how pediatricians should use them and what their limitations are. If you've ever wondered whether your child's doctor is using AI in any part of their care, this guidance is the starting point for that conversation.

The October 2026 issue of Pediatrics (the AAP's flagship journal) also published a study tracking trends in parent-reported developmental disabilities from 2019 to 2024. The data covers conditions like ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, and developmental delays — and how diagnosis patterns shifted across that five-year window, which included COVID-era disruptions to routine pediatric care.

On the research side, the conference featured studies linking smartphone ownership in young people to higher rates of depression, obesity, and insufficient sleep. None of these findings are entirely new, but having them consolidated in one conference is a signal that the AAP is treating screen-related health outcomes as a serious clinical issue, not just a lifestyle concern.

If you want to explore the AAP's resources on any of these topics, aap.org is the best starting point.

stories.title: The Gazette Endorses D11 Bond 4A — Follow-Up on Colorado Springs' Largest School Ballot Measure in Decades

x_posts.label: Post 5
x_posts.text:
The Gazette endorsed D11 Bond 4A today.

$775M for repairs at every D11 school — HVAC, asbestos removal, classroom upgrades, AC at Coronado High.

~$260/year for avg homeowner. Ballots in ~3 weeks.

#COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
Colorado Springs families, the Gazette editorial board came out in support of D11 Bond 4A today.

If you're just catching up: D11 has a $775 million bond measure on the November ballot — Ballot Question 4A. The district's board voted 6-1 to put it there back in August. It would fund repairs at every D11 school: new HVAC systems, asbestos removal, modernized classrooms, a full rebuild of one school, and — finally — air conditioning at Coronado High School.

It would be D11's first voter-approved bond since 2004.

The Gazette's endorsement is significant. It's the largest newspaper in Colorado Springs, and an editorial endorsement from them carries weight with a lot of voters who are still weighing the measure.

The cost to the average homeowner: approximately $260 per year. That's about $22 per month.

Ballots go out in about three weeks. If you want to review the full plan before yours arrives, d11.org/bond has the detailed breakdown.

What questions do you have about the D11 bond before voting?
